content:
# Semantic-Anchor Checkpoints for Stateless Seats

## 1. Coordinate layer (the memlang address space)

The context is not a token string. It is an ordered list of **segments** (the meta-tokens), and all addressing goes through coordinates, never raw offsets:

```
coord := (lineage: u64, ord: u32, Δtok: u32)
```

Every segment is content-addressed and carries its own token IDs:

```
Seg {
  sid        = H(canonical(content))     // content-addressed identity
  lineage, ord, kind                      // SYS|PERSONA|MEM_INJ|USER|ASSIST|
                                          // TOOL_CALL|TOOL_RESULT|SUMMARY|NOTE
  pos_base   : u32                        // first RoPE position (arena-allocated)
  n_tok      : u32
  tokens     : blob (u32 ids, zstd)       // PERSISTED, never re-tokenized
  prov       : [sid…]                     // provenance: summary→sources, result→call
  m_ord      = H(m_{ord-1} ‖ sid)         // incremental Merkle over segment IDs
}
```

Two invariants do all the work:

- **I1 (freeze discipline):** segments `[0 … last_sealed_ord]` are immutable. All edits land in the open suffix after the last anchor, or force a rebase (§4).
- **I2 (content-chained KV):** KV blocks are keyed by a hash chain over token content, so block validity is verifiable from the ledger alone, with no trust in pointers.

Why anchors must be *semantic* boundaries: a KV hash chain is all-or-nothing per prefix — an edit at token *t* kills every block at position ≥ *t*. Placing the anchor at a segment boundary means the killed set is exactly the segments being rewritten and nothing else. Alignment of edit points to anchor ordinals is the entire optimization.

## 2. Durable objects (exact formats)

**Anchor record** (one per seal):

```
Anchor {
  lineage, ord, prefix_digest = m_ord, n_tok_total,
  kv_manifest : [block_key…]   // chained keys covering tokens [0, n_tok_total)
  epoch, created_at
}
```

**KV block:**

```
key_i  = H(key_{i-1} ‖ pos_i ‖ tok_chunk_i)     // B = 64 tokens per block
val_i  = packed K/V for that span, all layers    // + H(val) checksum
```

Chained keys give you: (a) integrity — a block is usable iff its whole ancestor chain matches the ledger's tokens; (b) free cross-lineage/cross-agent sharing — identical prefixes (system + persona) produce identical keys automatically; (c) O(1) "how much prefix is warm" — probe the manifest deepest-first.

**Lineage pointer row:** `agent_id → (lineage, epoch, last_anchor_ord)`, updated by CAS on epoch. This is the only mutable pointer in the system.

**Tool-intent journal:** written *before* dispatch: `{intent_id = H(lineage, ord, payload), status: PENDING|DONE(result_sid), idempotency_key}`. Executors dedupe on `idempotency_key`, so a respawned seat re-dispatches safely.

**Write ordering:** ledger fsync → KV publish → anchor record. An anchor is trusted only after digest verification (§5), so stale/orphan KV is always harmless.

## 3. Persist vs. recompute — the core table

| | Disposition | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Segment ledger incl. **token IDs** | **Persist (fsync, source of truth)** | Persisting token IDs, not text, eliminates tokenizer drift and respawn re-tokenization entirely. Text is a debug projection. |
| Anchor records + KV manifests | **Persist** | Small (~hundreds of bytes each). |
| Lineage pointer + epoch | **Persist** | Single CAS row; fences dead seats. |
| Tool intents/results | **Persist** | Pre-dispatch WAL; idempotent replay. |
| KV blocks | **Persist best-effort** | Checksummed, evictable, tiered. Loss costs recompute, never correctness. |
| Prompt materialization | **Recompute** | Concatenation of persisted token arrays — O(N) memcpy, no model work. |
| KV for any missed block | **Recompute** | Prefill; hash chain tells you exactly which span. |
| Open (unsealed) suffix | **Always recompute** | Bounded by seal cadence C. |
| Embeddings / retrieval indexes | **Recompute** (persist only if rebuild is measurably expensive) | Derivable from ledger. |
| Sampler/RNG state | **Discarded by design** | See §6: respawn at turn boundaries makes this moot. |
| Partial decodes, speculative drafts | **Discarded** | Unsealed ⇒ not part of any checkpoint. |

Sizing honesty (7B-class, GQA 8 kv-heads, 32 layers, head_dim 128, fp16): 2·32·8·128·2 B = **131 KB/token**. A 128k context is ~17 GB of KV — so "persist everything forever" is wrong. Tier it: hot NVMe/distributed cache for the last K≈4 anchors' manifests; older anchors fall back to recompute-on-miss. Expected respawn re-prefill ≈ `open_suffix + p·(N − open_suffix)` where *p* is block-miss probability; the design drives *p*→0 for recent lineages and accepts compute for cold ones.

## 4. Edit protocols

**APPEND** — new segment in the open suffix. No invalidation. Auto-seal policy: seal an anchor when a turn finalizes, when a tool-result batch lands, or when open-suffix length exceeds **C ∈ [512, 2048]** tokens. Seal is O(1) amortized (Merkle maintained incrementally per append; only dirty tail blocks flush).

**EDIT(i…j)** — legal iff `i > last_sealed_ord`; otherwise rejected → REBASE. Rewritten span re-prefills against the nearest anchor's manifest; everything before survives byte-for-byte.

**COMPACT(a…b)** — touches frozen territory, so it's a **rebase**, executed as a shadow swap:

1. Build lineage L+1 in shadow: segments `[0…a)` copied **by reference** (same sids, same tokens ⇒ same block keys ⇒ same KV, zero recompute), one new SUMMARY segment (generated offline from `[a…b]` — a side pass that never disturbs the live context), segments `[b+1…end)` copied by reference.
2. Atomically CAS the lineage pointer L → L+1. Death before the swap leaves an orphan shadow (GC'd); after the swap it's just a normal lineage. Never half-applied.
3. Cost: only tokens from the summary insertion point onward re-prefill — once. Thereafter the summary is itself an anchored, cached prefix.

**Position handling (the hidden tax):** K/V has RoPE positions baked in, so shifting later tokens invalidates their blocks even if content is unchanged. Two policies:

- **Default:** re-run position allocation on rebase. Later segments miss once, recompute, restabilize. Simple, always correct.
- **Optimization — position arenas:** allocate each segment a reserved stride `base_{i+1} = base_i + max(n_tok_i + slack, floor)` with non-contiguous positions across gaps. Edits that grow a segment within its slack leave all later positions untouched ⇒ later blocks stay valid; compaction leaves a position gap where merged segments lived. RoPE tolerates gaps, but gap-size distribution shift is model-dependent — gate behind eval, fall back to default. This is the mechanism that makes "suffix-only re-prefill" hold even for mid-context edits.

## 5. Respawn algorithm (exact)

```
respawn(agent):
 1. (L, e') ← CAS_bump_epoch(agent_id)          # fence the dead seat
 2. A ← newest anchor(L) that VERIFIES:
      rebuild m_ord from ledger; require m_ord == A.prefix_digest
      on mismatch, walk to previous anchor       # self-healing; ledger is append-only
 3. d ← deepest prefix of A.kv_manifest present in block store
      (parallel HEAD + checksum; chain guarantees monotone availability)
 4. sealed_toks  ← concat(tokens[0 … A.ord])     # pure memcpy of persisted IDs
    suffix_toks ← concat(tokens[A.ord … head])   # small by seal-cadence bound
 5. prefill(sealed_toks[d·B :], then suffix_toks),
    publishing chained blocks as computed
 6. re-record anchor at same ord (digest identical ⇒ idempotent refresh of manifest)
 7. re-dispatch journal[PENDING] intents with original idempotency keys
 8. resume the agent loop at the turn boundary
```

Cold cost: full prefill, O(N). Warm cost: `suffix + evicted span` only. Verification in step 2 is what replaces distributed transactions — crash consistency comes from append-only ledger + hash-checked anchors, not from locking.

## 6. Death semantics and the sampling problem

A seat that dies mid-generation loses its unsealed decode — deliberately. Redo is bounded by C. The two nasty cases are handled structurally:

- **Mid-tool-call death:** intent was journalled pre-dispatch; respawn replays with the same idempotency key. No duplicate side effects, no lost effects.
- **Mid-decode death:** partial tokens are discarded; the orchestrator re-issues the turn. Bit-exact continuation across respawn is *not* guaranteed (nondeterministic kernels) and is not the goal — the goal is **semantic continuity**, achieved by preferring kill-at-anchor: drain to the next seal before evicting a seat. At a turn boundary there is no sampler state to lose and divergence is unobservable.

## 7. memlang op surface (what the agent/runtime actually calls)

```
APPEND(kind, payload)            → sid          # suffix only
SEAL()                           → anchor       # idempotent at current tail
EDIT(ord_range, patch)           → ok | REBASE_REQUIRED
COMPACT(a, b, summarizer)        → new_lineage  # atomic pointer swap
FORK(tag)                        → lineage'     # speculative branches: prefix blocks shared free
ATTACH(sids)                     → sid          # memory injections as first-class provenance-tracked segments
RESOLVE(handle "@step12.result") → coord        # references compile to (lineage, ord, Δtok)+sid,
                                                # so they survive appends and map through compaction
```

Agent-visible handles bind to `sid`, never to offsets — that's what makes references stable across edits. GC rule: a segment leaves the *active* context only when summarized and unreferenced by any live segment's `prov`; the ledger retains everything for audit and fork.

## Summary of the design's load-bearing choices

1. **Segments (meta-tokens) with persisted token IDs** — respawn never re-tokenizes; coordinates survive edits.
2. **Freeze-at-anchor discipline** — edits hit the open suffix by construction; compaction is an atomic rebase, not an in-place mutation.
3. **Content-chained KV blocks** — validity is checkable from the ledger alone; cache loss degrades to compute, never to corruption; identical prefixes dedupe across seats for free.
4. **Hash-verified anchors instead of transactions** — append-only ledger + Merkle digest = crash consistency with zero coordination.
5. **Pre-dispatch intent journaling + idempotency keys** — tool effects survive death exactly once.
6. **Kill-at-anchor preference** — converts the sampler-state problem into a non-problem.

Persist: ledger, anchors, pointer/epoch, intents, best-effort KV. Recompute: assembly (memcpy), misses, open suffix, derived indexes. Discard: unsealed decodes. Nothing else exists.
reasoning:
The user is asking about a hard systems design problem: semantic-anchor checkpoints for an agent's context edit re-prefill mechanism, in a "memlang / meta-token coordinate layer," designed for a stateless seat (agent instance) that dies and respawns. They want concrete, exact, grounded design — what persists vs what recomputes.

Let me parse the domain. This is about LLM serving infrastructure and agent runtime design:

1. **Context edit re-prefill**: When an agent's context window gets edited (e.g., compaction/summarization of old turns, tool result truncation, memory injection), you don't want to re-prefill the entire context from scratch. You want to reuse KV cache for the unchanged prefix and only prefill the new suffix.

2. **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: Checkpoints placed at semantically meaningful boundaries (not arbitrary token positions) so that when an edit happens, the invalidation boundary aligns with a checkpoint, maximizing prefix-cache hits.

3. **memlang / meta-token coordinate layer**: This sounds like a virtualized coordinate system over the context — a logical address space where "meta-tokens" are units above raw tokens (e.g., a message, a tool call block, a summary segment). "memlang" suggests a language/grammar for memory operations — addressing, referencing, versioning segments of context. The coordinate layer maps logical coordinates → physical token spans → KV cache blocks.

4. **Stateless seat that dies and respawns**: The agent process is ephemeral. It can be killed at any time and respawned elsewhere. So all state must either persist durably or be recomputable deterministically from persisted inputs. This is like a stateless worker with externalized state.

So the design must specify:
- The coordinate system (meta-token space)
- What a semantic anchor is, where they're placed, how they're identified
- The checkpoint record format
- The persistence layer: what's written to durable storage vs derived on respawn
- The respawn/recovery procedure: how the new seat reconstructs enough state to continue with minimal recompute
- The edit protocol: how an edit invalidates suffixes and triggers partial re-prefill
- Cache keying: how KV cache blocks are addressed so a respawned seat can hit warm cache from another process (prefix caching across processes via shared cache keyed by content hash)

Let me build this concretely.

## Core model

**Coordinate layer**: Define a logical context as an ordered sequence of *segments* (the meta-tokens). Each segment has:
- `seg_id`: content-addressed hash (e.g., SHA-256 of canonical serialization) — actually better: `(role, kind, content_hash)` so identical content dedupes.
- `span`: token range [start, end) in the materialized prompt — but since edits shift offsets, we should NOT use absolute token offsets as primary keys; use ordinal position in the segment list + content hash. Token offsets are derived.
- `kind`: system / persona / memory-injection / user-turn / assistant-turn / tool-call / tool-result / summary / scratchpad.
- `deps`: which prior segments it was conditioned on (for summaries: source segment IDs; for tool results: call ID).

**Anchors**: A semantic anchor is a designated segment boundary that is a valid resynchronization point: everything strictly before the anchor is immutable-append-only (frozen), everything after is mutable. Anchors are chosen at natural freeze points: end of system+persona block, end of each committed turn, end of a compaction boundary, end of a memory injection batch.

Key invariant: **prefix immutability up to the last sealed anchor**. Edits only ever rewrite the open suffix after the last anchor. If an edit must touch frozen territory (e.g., re-summarize older history), that's a *rebase*: you create a new lineage/fork of the context with a new root, and old checkpoints remain valid for the old lineage but the new lineage starts fresh at the rebase point — except you can seed the new lineage's first checkpoint by pointing at the cached KV of the summary text if it's byte-identical to something already cached (content-addressed cache makes this free).

**Checkpoints**: A checkpoint captures enough to resume prefill at an anchor without recomputing anything before it. In a transformer serving stack, the true reusable artifact is the KV cache. Two levels:

1. **Logical checkpoint (durable, small)**: `{lineage_id, anchor_ordinal, seg_list_hash_prefix, kv_ref}` where `kv_ref` points into a content-addressed KV store.
2. **Physical KV blocks (durable-ish, evictable)**: paged KV blocks keyed by `hash(parent_block_key || token_chunk)` — standard prefix-cache chaining (like vLLM's automatic prefix caching / SGLang RadixAttention). Block keys form a Merkle chain, so any block is valid iff its whole ancestor chain hashes match — this gives integrity without trusting pointers.

**What persists vs recomputes** — the crux. Let me enumerate precisely.

### Persists (durable write-ahead log + object store)

1. **Segment ledger (append-only)**: every segment ever appended, with `seg_id`, `kind`, `ordinal` within lineage, `parent_lineage` if rebased, `created_at`, `token_len`. Content stored once (dedup by hash). This is the memlang address space ground truth. Small: bytes per segment metadata, content blobs.

2. **Anchor registry**: per lineage, the ordinals that are anchors, plus seal records: `{anchor_ordinal, seg_prefix_digest, kv_root_block_key, token_count}`. The `seg_prefix_digest` = Merkle root over segment IDs [0..anchor_ordinal). This lets a respawned seat verify "my view of history matches the checkpointed one" in O(1) compare.

3. **KV block store**: paged KV tensors keyed by chained hash. Written through on each anchor seal (and opportunistically between anchors). Evictable — losing blocks costs recompute, not correctness. Store per-block: key, layer count × heads × head_dim × 2 (K,V), dtype, seq positions covered. Position metadata matters because RoPE positions are baked into K/V; the block key must include absolute position base to avoid collisions after edits shift things — see below on position handling.

4. **Seat lease/intent record**: tiny row saying which seat owns the lineage, epoch number, heartbeat. For fencing: a respawned seat bumps epoch; stale seats' writes are rejected by epoch check. Prevents split-brain double-append.

5. **Open-suffix intent (optional micro-journal)**: if the seat dies mid-generation, the partially generated tokens are just discarded — they're recomputed by re-decoding from the last anchor (or last sealed turn). Optionally journal sampled tokens every N tokens to shorten redo, but simplest correct answer: discard; decode redo is cheap relative to prefill redo only if suffix is short — cap open suffix length to make redo bounded (e.g., force anchor seal every ≤2k tokens).

### Recomputes on respawn

1. **Materialized prompt assembly**: replay ledger → ordered segment list → tokenize → token array. Deterministic given ledger. Cost: O(context tokens) CPU for detokenize/retokenize glue — but note: you should persist the *tokenization* too, or rather persist segments in token-space (store token IDs, not just text) to avoid tokenizer drift and re-tokenization cost. Better: **persist token IDs per segment**. Then respawn concatenates token arrays — no tokenizer invocation at all. Text is a projection for humans/debugging.

2. **KV for unsealed suffix**: any tokens after the last sealed anchor's KV simply get prefilled again. Bounded by the anchor cadence policy.

3. **Anything whose KV blocks were evicted**: re-prefill that span. Correctness never depends on cache presence because block validity is verified by hash chain against the token content — a miss degrades to compute.

4. **Derived indexes** (e.g., embedding index over segments for retrieval): rebuildable from ledger; don't persist unless rebuild is expensive — mark as "persist-if-large."

### The edit protocol

Edits come in kinds, each with defined invalidation semantics:

- **Append** (new turn/tool result): extends suffix. No invalidation. New tokens prefill against last anchor's KV tail. Actually careful: prefill of appended tokens needs the KV of ALL preceding tokens; that's exactly the sealed anchor's KV root chain. Fine.
- **Suffix rewrite** (edit/extend the open turn, inject memory into the open zone): invalidate from the earliest edited segment ordinal to end; re-prefill that span using anchor KV before it. If the earliest edit point is itself an anchor boundary, zero waste beyond the edited span.
- **Compaction** (replace segments [a..b] with a summary segment): this touches frozen territory → **rebase**. Procedure: create lineage L+1; new segment list = [0..a) copied by reference (same seg_ids, same token content → same block keys → same KV!) + [summary_seg] + [b+1..end) copied by reference. Because blocks are content-chained, the prefix [0..a) KV is reused verbatim; only the summary insertion point onward re-prefills. The summary segment itself: its tokens are new, so its KV is computed once and then becomes reusable for all future appends. Crucially, the summary generation itself can be done as a separate pass reading [a..b] — that's a side computation, doesn't disturb the live context until committed atomically via a lineage pointer swap.
- **Position remap problem**: inserting/deleting tokens shifts RoPE positions of everything after. Two options: (a) accept re-prefill of shifted region (positions baked in K/V); (b) use position-independent tricks. Concrete answer: bake `position_base` into the block key namespace per lineage-segment-run: i.e., block key = H(lineage, run_start_pos, chunk_index, token_chunk). After a rebase, segments after the summary get NEW positions → their old blocks are dead weight under new keys; they'll miss and recompute once, then re-stabilize. Alternative that avoids this: allocate positions with gaps (position stride reservation, e.g., each segment reserves a fixed position budget like 4096 slots regardless of actual length) so insertions within budget don't shift later segments' positions. That's a real technique (like virtual position arenas). Trade-off: wastes RoPE range; with YaRN-style scaling or long-context RoPE budgets it's affordable. I should present both: default = accept one-time recompute on rebase; optimization = position arena with reserved strides for hot-edit zones.

Actually let me think harder about the position arena idea because it's central to making edits cheap. If every segment gets a reserved position slot range [i*S, (i+1)*S), then editing segment i's content keeps segments >i at identical positions → their KV remains valid → edit cost = re-prefill of segment i only. Compaction merges several segments into one summary placed in the union of their slots... hmm, merging breaks it unless the summary takes the first slot and freed slots are just skipped (positions need not be contiguous! RoPE works fine with non-contiguous positions; attention doesn't care about gaps, though models trained on contiguous text may degrade slightly with large gaps — mitigate by keeping gap sizes moderate or using attention-with-position-buckets). This is a genuinely useful design lever: **non-contiguous position allocation with per-segment arenas**. I'll include it as the mechanism that makes "suffix-only re-prefill" hold even for mid-context edits, with the caveat about distribution shift and the fallback.

But wait — the question says "context edit re-prefills only the new suffix." So the target guarantee: any edit ⇒ re-prefill ⊆ tokens after the nearest surviving anchor before the edit point. With append-only-until-anchor discipline, edits land in the open suffix by construction; compaction is the exception handled by rebase + content-addressed reuse. Good.

### Anchor placement policy

Seal an anchor when:
- A turn completes (assistant message finalized).
- A tool-result batch lands.
- Open suffix exceeds T_max tokens (force seal; if mid-generation, seal at next stop).
- Before any operation that might rewrite history (pre-compaction seal).
Each seal writes: anchor record {ordinal, prefix_digest, kv_root_key, n_tokens} + flushes dirty KV blocks. Seals are idempotent (keyed by ordinal+digest).

Also **micro-anchors inside long tool results?** Not needed if tool results are single segments; granularity = segment. Keep it simple: anchor == segment boundary flagged sealed.

### Respawn procedure (exact steps)

New seat boot:
1. Read lineage pointer (current lineage id + epoch). CAS-claim: bump epoch, fence old seat.
2. Load anchor registry for lineage; take max sealed anchor A.
3. Verify: recompute Merkle digest over segment ids [0..A.ordinal] from ledger; must equal A.prefix_digest. Mismatch ⇒ ledger/checkpoint divergence ⇒ fall back to previous anchor (walk back until verify passes; ledger is append-only so earlier anchors verify). This gives self-healing integrity.
4. Probe KV store for A.kv_root_key chain presence (HEAD requests on block keys — cheap). Count available depth. Blocks are chained, so availability is monotone from root: find deepest available descendant along expected chain... actually chain is a tree (each block's key includes parent), so from root you can walk while children exist. Simpler: store at anchor a manifest of block keys in order; probe them; find longest available prefix run. Re-prefill from there.
5. Assemble token array: concat persisted token-ID arrays of segments [0..current_end). Segments after A: their tokens go into the re-prefill buffer.
6. Prefill missing span (from deepest available block boundary to end of sealed region + open suffix), writing new blocks with chained keys as it goes; re-seal anchor A′ at same ordinal with new kv_root if blocks were rebuilt (idempotent overwrite keyed by digest — digest identical since tokens identical, so it's just refreshing kv_root_key mapping; keep both roots valid).
7. Resume decoding.

Cost accounting on respawn: cold = full prefill O(N). Warm = prefill O(open_suffix + evicted_span). With anchor cadence C tokens and eviction probability p, expected re-prefill ≈ open_suffix + p·(N − open_suffix). Persisting KV to disk/NVM (or relying on a shared serving-layer prefix cache with sufficient capacity) drives p→0 for recent lineages.

### Where does KV live?

Options, concrete:
- **Same-process radix cache**: useless across death (stateless seat) unless the serving fleet shares a distributed prefix cache. So: KV blocks go to a shared object store / Redis-tier with RDMA or local NVMe cache fronting. Block size ~ page (e.g., 16–128 tokens). Write-through on seal; write-behind allowed between seals (loss = recompute).
- Integrity: chained-content hashing means a corrupted/mismatched block is detected at attach time (verify hash of the token chunk that produced it — you have the tokens from the ledger, so verification is: does stored block's recorded token_chunk hash match ledger tokens? K/V themselves can carry a checksum).

Hmm, verifying K/V tensor integrity: store `H(block_kv_bytes)` alongside; on load, checksum. Cheap.

### memlang surface

Give the coordinate layer an actual grammar — the question explicitly says "in the memlang / meta-token coordinate layer." So define ops:

```
ctx := {lineage, segs[]}
segs[i] := {sid, kind, pos_arena, tokens[], sealed}
ops:
  APPEND(kind, payload) -> sid            # suffix only
  SEAL(at=tail) -> anchor{ord, digest, kvroot}
  EDIT(ord_range, patch)                  # legal only if min(ord_range) > last_sealed_ord, else REBASE required
  COMPACT(a,b, summarizer) -> new_lineage # atomic swap
  FORK(tag) -> new lineage handle         # speculative branches share prefix blocks free
  ATTACH(sid_set)                         # memory injections as first-class segments with provenance
```

Meta-token = segment; coordinates = (lineage, ordinal, intra-seg token offset). All agent references to context ("that result from step 12") resolve through coords, never raw offsets — this is what makes edits safe: references survive insertion because ordinals of untouched segments are stable under append, and under compaction the ledger keeps old sids resolvable (mapped to "summarized into sid_s").

Provenance edges: summary segment stores `sources=[sids]`; tool result stores `call=sid`. Enables garbage collection: a segment is droppable from active context when no live segment depends on it AND it's summarized — but ledger retains forever (audit).

### Failure matrix

- Die mid-append before seal: suffix discarded, re-append from client/agent replay? No — the agent's own intent: the turn being generated is lost; respawn resumes from last anchor; the orchestrator re-issues the pending action. To avoid duplicate tool execution: tool calls are journaled in ledger BEFORE dispatch (intent record), and results idempotent-keyed; respawn sees intent-without-result and re-dispatches with same idempotency key. That's important and concrete: **write-ahead the tool intent, execute with idempotency key = H(lineage, ordinal, payload)**.
- Die mid-compaction: compaction is staged: build new lineage fully (segments + summary + sealed anchor) in shadow, then single pointer swap (CAS lineage ref). Death before swap = orphan shadow, GC later; after swap = normal. Never half-applied.
- Ledger write succeeds but KV lost: fine, recompute path.
- KV present but ledger rolled back (shouldn't happen with append-only + fsync ordering): order writes: ledger fsync → then KV publish → then anchor record. Anchor record references both; recovery trusts anchor only after verifying digest, so stale KV is harmless.

### Sizes/latencies (ground it)

- Segment metadata ~200B; ledger for 100k-segment lifetime ~20MB. Trivial.
- KV per token: for a 7B-class model (32 layers, GQA 8 kv-heads, head_dim 128, fp16): 2·32·8·128·2B = 131KB/token. 128k context ≈ 17GB. So full-context durable KV is heavy → block-level dedup + eviction tiering matters; hot tail on NVMe, cold recompute acceptable. For MoE/big models worse. State numbers honestly: persisting all KV always is usually wrong; persist sealed-region KV with LRU tiers, budget e.g. last 4 checkpoints hot.
- Seal latency: digest over prefix incremental (Merkle maintained incrementally per append) → O(1) amortized; KV flush of dirty tail pages only.

### What persists vs recomputes — final crisp table

Persist (source of truth):
1. Segment ledger w/ token IDs (append-only, fsync'd) 
2. Anchor records (ordinal, prefix Merkle digest, kv_root manifest)
3. Lineage pointer + epoch (single CAS row)
4. Tool-intent journal entries (pre-dispatch)
5. KV blocks (best-effort, checksummed, evictable, content-chained)

Recompute:
1. Prompt materialization (concat of persisted token arrays — near-free, no tokenizer)
2. Any KV not found (prefill)
3. Open suffix (unsealed tokens) — always
4. Derived artifacts: embeddings, retrieval indexes, caches of summarizer outputs (optional persist)
5. Decoder RNG stream / sampling state: define determinism policy — persist seed + position; on respawn, sampling continues from re-decoded logits; exact continuation requires deterministic kernels or accept divergence after respawn (state it: bit-exactness across respawn is NOT guaranteed unless kernels deterministic; policy choice: "semantic continuity" not "token continuity" — the seat resumes at a turn boundary whenever possible so divergence is invisible).

That last point is subtle and worth stating: respawn ideally happens at anchor boundaries (between turns), where "what the agent would have said next" hasn't started; then no sampling-state problem at all. Mid-generation death ⇒ discard partial decode, redo the turn. So the seat's kill policy should prefer kill-at-anchor (drain to anchor before eviction) — makes respawn clean. Stateless seat + cooperative checkpointing.

### Edge details worth including

- Tokenizer stability: persist token IDs ⇒ immune to tokenizer updates; version-tag anyway.

**Segment record (ledger entry):**
```
Seg {
  sid        : H(canonical(content))          // content-addressed
  lineage    : u64
  ord        : u32                            // ordinal within lineage
  kind       : enum {SYS, PERSONA, MEM_INJ, USER, ASSIST, TOOL_CALL, TOOL_RESULT, SUMMARY, NOTE}
  pos_base   : u32                            // first RoPE position (arena-allocated)
  n_tok      : u32
  tokens     : blob (u32 ids, zstd)           // persisted, not re-derived
  text       : blob (optional, debug)
  prov       : [sid...]                       // sources/call refs
  prev_ord_digest : H(...)                    // incremental Merkle: m_i = H(m_{i-1} || sid_i)
}
```
Incremental Merkle over sids gives prefix digest at any ordinal in O(1) from last entry. 

**Anchor record:**
```
Anchor {
  lineage, ord, prefix_digest (=m_ord), n_tok_total,
  kv_manifest : [block_key...]   // chained keys covering tokens [0..n_tok_total)
  created_at, epoch
}
```

**Block:**
```
Block {
  key = H(prev_key || pos || tok_chunk(B))
  val = packed K/V for its token span, all layers
  checksum = H(val)
}
```
B = 64 tokens say. Note: block boundaries must align to segment-independent global token grid per run; grid resets at run boundaries (pos_base changes). Fine.

Wait, one subtlety: chained block keys mean to look up "do I have KV for prefix ending at block k" you just probe key_k. Manifest lists them in order; binary search deepest available via probing — probes are O(log n) with a sorted structure or just linear scan of manifest HEAD checks (cheap, parallel). Fine.

**Lineage pointer row:** `{agent_id -> (lineage, epoch, last_anchor_ord)}`, CAS on epoch.

**Tool intent journal:** `{intent_id = H(lineage, ord, payload_hash), status: PENDING|DONE(result_sid), idempotency_key}` — written before dispatch; executor dedupes on idempotency_key.

**Respawn algorithm:**
```
respawn(agent):
  (L, e') = CAS_bump_epoch(agent)             // fence old seat
  A = latest verifiable anchor(L):             // walk anchors newest→oldest,
      for each: rebuild m_ord from ledger, require == prefix_digest
  blocks = longest_available_prefix(A.kv_manifest)   // parallel HEAD+checksum
  toks = concat(tokens[0..A.ord])              // sealed region
  tail = concat(tokens[A.ord..head])           // unsealed suffix (usually small)
  pending_intents = journal[PENDING]           // re-dispatch w/ same idem key
  prefill(from=blocks.depth, toks=toks[tail_start:] + tail)
  republish missing blocks; re-record anchor (same digest, new manifest)
  resume loop at turn boundary
```

**Edit rules:**
- APPEND: allowed anytime; auto-seal policy triggers.
- EDIT(i..j): require i > last_sealed_ord else reject→REBASE.
- COMPACT(a..b): shadow-build lineage L+1: copy segs [0..a) by reference (same sids/tokens/blocks), SUMMARY seg (generated off-line from [a..b]), copy [b+1..end). Positions: default re-run allocation (later segs get new pos_base ⇒ their blocks miss once, recompute); optimized: arena strides. Swap pointer atomically. Old lineage retained read-only (fork/audit/GC later).

Position arena option detail: `pos(seg_i) = base_i + offset`, base_{i+1} = base_i + stride_i where stride_i ≥ n_tok_i, extra slack for growth (e.g., slack = min(1024, n_tok)). Edits growing a segment within slack keep later positions stable ⇒ later blocks stay valid. Compaction places summary at base_a, frees [base_a+stride_summary .. base_b+stride_b] as a gap — non-contiguous positions. Caveat: RoPE gap robustness varies by model; gate behind eval; fallback = re-run allocation.

**Persist-vs-recompute table** — make it the centerpiece, exact.

PERSIST (fsync, source of truth):
- ledger segments incl. token IDs
- anchor records + manifests
- lineage pointer/epoch
- tool intents + results
- (best-effort) KV blocks

RECOMPUTE:
- prompt assembly (concat; O(N) memcpy)
- KV misses (prefill)
- open suffix always
- embeddings/indexes
- sampler state (policy: resume at boundaries; mid-gen death discards)

NEITHER (discarded by design):
- unsealed partial decodes
- ephemeral attention buffers
- speculative drafts

Also mention: why anchors at semantic boundaries matter mechanically — because block-chain validity is all-or-nothing per prefix; an edit at token t kills all blocks ≥ t. Aligning t with a segment boundary means the killed set = exactly the segments being rewritten; semantic alignment maximizes survivor set.
